text: Adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week, such as brisk walking, or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity, or an equivalent combination. Adults also need muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days each week. Activity can be spread across the week and broken into smaller amounts of time. Some physical activity is better than none, and adults who sit less and do any moderate- or vigorous-intensity activity gain health benefits. Adults can choose activities that fit daily life, spread activity across the week, and build up gradually while keeping activity at an appropriate intensity for their health and ability.

source_title: Adding Physical Activity as an Adult
text: Adults can add physical activity in many ways. Any aerobic activity counts if it is done at moderate or vigorous intensity, and any amount of physical activity has some health benefits. Weekly activity can be divided into shorter sessions, such as 30 minutes a day for 5 days. Planning goals, choosing activities that fit daily life, and finding ways to stay on track can help adults make physical activity a regular habit. Adults can choose activities that fit daily life, spread activity across the week, and build up gradually while keeping activity at an appropriate intensity for their health and ability.

source_title: What Counts as Physical Activity for Adults
text: Aerobic physical activity, sometimes called cardio, gets a person breathing harder and makes the heart beat faster. Moderate- or vigorous-intensity activity counts toward adult aerobic activity guidelines. Adults can meet weekly recommendations through 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity, 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity, or a combination. The activity does not have to be completed all at once and can be spread across the week in shorter sessions. Adults can choose activities that fit daily life, spread activity across the week, and build up gradually while keeping activity at an appropriate intensity for their health and ability.

source_title: Physical Activity and Your Weight and Health
text: Regular physical activity provides immediate and long-term health benefits. It can improve brain health, strengthen bones and muscles, improve ability to perform everyday activities, and improve sleep quality. It can also reduce high blood pressure, reduce risk of heart disease and stroke, reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, reduce arthritis pain and disability, and reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety. Physical activity is important for overall health and for maintaining a healthy weight. Adults can choose activities that fit daily life, spread activity across the week, and build up gradually while keeping activity at an appropriate intensity for their health and ability.

Physical activity includes all movement produced by skeletal muscles that uses energy. It includes walking, cycling, wheeling, sports, active recreation, play, household chores, and physical work. Regular physical activity helps prevent and manage noncommunicable diseases such as heart disease, hypertension, stroke, diabetes, and several cancers. It also helps maintain a healthy body weight and can improve mental health, quality of life, and well-being. Adults can choose activities that fit daily life, spread activity across the week, and build up gradually while keeping activity at an appropriate intensity for their health and ability.

source_title: Steps for Getting Started With Physical Activity
text: Regular physical activity is one of the most important things people can do for health. Immediate benefits include better sleep, reduced anxiety, and lower blood pressure. Regular activity can also lower the chances of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers. People with chronic conditions may want to talk with a health care provider about the right types and amounts of physical activity. Adults can begin by splitting weekly activity into manageable daily amounts. Adults can choose activities that fit daily life, spread activity across the week, and build up gradually while keeping activity at an appropriate intensity for their health and ability.

A healthy diet supports health, well-being, growth, and development. Evidence shows health benefits from diets high in whole grains, vegetables, fruit, legumes, and nuts, and low in salt, free sugars, and fats, especially saturated and trans fats. Unhealthy diet is a leading risk for noncommunicable diseases such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and cancer. Healthy dietary patterns can protect against malnutrition and support lifelong health. A healthy pattern should be based on variety and should limit salt, added or free sugars, saturated fat, and trans fat as part of overall disease prevention.

A healthy diet includes a combination of different foods, including staples such as cereals or starchy roots, legumes such as lentils and beans, fruit and vegetables, and foods from animal sources such as meat, fish, eggs, and milk. Eating a variety of foods and consuming less salt, sugars, saturated fats, and industrially produced trans fats are important parts of a healthy diet. A healthy pattern should be based on variety and should limit salt, added or free sugars, saturated fat, and trans fat as part of overall disease prevention.

Healthy eating can include more fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and lower-fat dairy choices, while limiting added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium. People can make changes by reading nutrition labels, choosing foods with lower amounts of added sugars or sodium, drinking water instead of sugary drinks, and replacing sugary snacks with fruit or vegetable slices. Small changes to everyday food choices can support healthier eating patterns. A healthy pattern should be based on variety and should limit salt, added or free sugars, saturated fat, and trans fat as part of overall disease prevention.

For people living with diabetes or diabetes risk, healthy eating can include choosing carbohydrates that are higher in fiber and lower in added sugar, such as beans and sweet potatoes, and limiting sugary drinks and highly processed snack foods. Drinking more water and fewer sweetened beverages can reduce added sugars and blood sugar swings. Meal choices can be adapted to personal preferences and daily life while supporting weight and blood sugar goals. A healthy pattern should be based on variety and should limit salt, added or free sugars, saturated fat, and trans fat as part of overall disease prevention.

A healthy dietary pattern is low in salt, free sugars, and fats, particularly saturated and trans fats. Diets high in whole grains, fruit, vegetables, legumes, and nuts are associated with health benefits. Reducing salt, sugars, and unhealthy fats is part of preventing diet-related noncommunicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Healthy diets begin early in life and support health across the lifespan. A healthy pattern should be based on variety and should limit salt, added or free sugars, saturated fat, and trans fat as part of overall disease prevention.

Nutrition labels can help people identify foods with lower amounts of added sugars and sodium. To limit added sugars, people can choose water instead of sugary drinks, add fruit for sweetness, choose fruit and vegetable slices for snacks, and avoid flavored syrups in coffee drinks. To reduce sodium, people can compare packaged foods, choose lower-sodium options, and be aware that packaged and prepared foods are major sodium sources. A healthy pattern should be based on variety and should limit salt, added or free sugars, saturated fat, and trans fat as part of overall disease prevention.

Healthy weight loss includes a lifestyle with healthy eating patterns, regular physical activity, enough sleep, and stress management. People who lose weight at a gradual, steady pace, about 1 to 2 pounds per week, are more likely to keep weight off than people who lose weight more quickly. A specific plan can help people get started, and weight management can be affected by medicines, medical conditions, stress, genes, hormones, environment, and age. Sustainable weight management should be based on ongoing healthy eating patterns, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and realistic goals rather than short-term extreme changes.

source_title: Physical Activity and Your Weight and Health
text: Physical activity helps use calories for energy. Combined with reducing calories from food and drinks, physical activity can help create the calorie deficit needed for weight loss. Most weight loss comes from reducing calories, but regular physical activity is important for maintaining weight loss. Reaching and staying at a healthy weight requires both regular physical activity and healthy eating patterns. Sustainable weight management should be based on ongoing healthy eating patterns, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and realistic goals rather than short-term extreme changes.

Body mass index and waist circumference are two ways to get an idea of whether weight is in a healthy range. Losing weight does not have to mean losing a large amount. The details of a weight plan depend on what a person likes and what fits daily life. People who need ideas and support can talk with a registered dietitian, diabetes educator, or health care provider for guidance that matches their health needs. Sustainable weight management should be based on ongoing healthy eating patterns, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and realistic goals rather than short-term extreme changes.

A weight management plan can start with clear goals, realistic changes, and daily habits that support nutrition, activity, sleep, and stress management. Healthy weight loss should avoid unrealistic short-term promises and focus on sustainable changes that a person can continue. People concerned about weight or who have questions about medicines or medical conditions that affect weight should discuss them with a health care provider. Sustainable weight management should be based on ongoing healthy eating patterns, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and realistic goals rather than short-term extreme changes.

source_title: Physical Activity and Your Weight and Health
text: The amount of physical activity needed to maintain a healthy weight varies from person to person. For general health, adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week or an equivalent amount of vigorous activity, along with muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days each week. To lose weight and keep it off, people generally need regular physical activity together with healthy eating patterns. Sustainable weight management should be based on ongoing healthy eating patterns, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and realistic goals rather than short-term extreme changes.

Healthy living habits can help prevent high blood pressure and its complications. CDC recommends healthy meal and snack options with plenty of fresh fruits and vegetables, foods rich in potassium, fiber, and protein, and foods lower in salt and saturated fat. Reaching or maintaining a healthy weight, choosing healthy foods, getting regular physical activity, not smoking, limiting alcohol, and getting enough sleep can support blood pressure and heart health. Lifestyle habits that support blood pressure include healthier eating, regular activity, weight management when needed, not smoking, limiting alcohol, and adequate sleep.

High blood pressure, also called hypertension, is blood pressure that is higher than normal and is consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg. High blood pressure typically has no signs or symptoms, but it can affect the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes. People can take steps each day to keep blood pressure in a healthy range, and some people may be able to control blood pressure through lifestyle changes or blood pressure medicines. Lifestyle habits that support blood pressure include healthier eating, regular activity, weight management when needed, not smoking, limiting alcohol, and adequate sleep.

High blood pressure risk can be affected by health conditions, lifestyle, and family history. Physical inactivity, an unhealthy diet, and medical conditions such as diabetes can increase risk. Behaviors such as drinking too much alcohol and using tobacco can also increase risk. Some risk factors, including age and family history, cannot be controlled, but people can take steps to change controllable factors. Lifestyle habits that support blood pressure include healthier eating, regular activity, weight management when needed, not smoking, limiting alcohol, and adequate sleep.

To help prevent high blood pressure, CDC recommends discussing with a health care team ways to reach a healthy weight, including choosing healthy foods and getting regular physical activity. CDC also identifies not smoking, limiting alcohol, and getting enough sleep as healthy habits related to blood pressure and heart health. Lifestyle advice for people with high blood pressure should emphasize gradual, sustainable changes and awareness of individual health needs. Lifestyle habits that support blood pressure include healthier eating, regular activity, weight management when needed, not smoking, limiting alcohol, and adequate sleep.

For blood pressure prevention, CDC recommends talking with a health care team about eating a variety of foods that are rich in potassium, fiber, and protein and lower in salt, also called sodium, and saturated fat. Choosing healthy meal and snack options, eating plenty of fresh fruits and vegetables, and reducing high-sodium foods can help support blood pressure and protect against heart disease and stroke. Sodium reduction is best treated as part of a broader healthy eating pattern that emphasizes fresh foods, nutrition label use, and lower-sodium packaged or prepared options.

Eating too much sodium can raise the risk of high blood pressure, heart attack, and stroke. More than 70 percent of sodium consumed in the United States comes from packaged and prepared foods. Sodium has many forms, and most sodium consumed is from salt. People can reduce sodium by reading nutrition labels, comparing packaged foods, and choosing lower-sodium options when available. Sodium reduction is best treated as part of a broader healthy eating pattern that emphasizes fresh foods, nutrition label use, and lower-sodium packaged or prepared options.

A healthy diet is low in salt and supports prevention of diet-related noncommunicable diseases, including cardiovascular diseases and diabetes. WHO describes evidence of health benefits from diets high in whole grains, vegetables, fruit, legumes, and nuts and low in salt, free sugars, and unhealthy fats. Reducing salt intake is part of an overall healthy dietary pattern rather than a single isolated change. Sodium reduction is best treated as part of a broader healthy eating pattern that emphasizes fresh foods, nutrition label use, and lower-sodium packaged or prepared options.

Prediabetes and type 2 diabetes share many risk factors. Risk is higher for people who have overweight or obesity, are age 45 or older, have a parent or sibling with type 2 diabetes, are physically active less than 3 times a week, or have a history of gestational diabetes. Some behavior changes can lower risk, including increasing physical activity, eating a healthy diet, and losing weight if a person has overweight or obesity. Diabetes prevention guidance emphasizes healthy eating, regular physical activity, weight management when needed, and gradual behavior changes that can be maintained over time.

Regular physical activity is a foundation of diabetes management and can help manage blood sugar levels while lowering risk of heart disease and other complications. CDC suggests that people can start slowly rather than spending hours at a gym. A clear goal, such as taking a 10-minute walk after dinner, can help build activity. The weekly goal is at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity, with activity built up gradually. Diabetes prevention guidance emphasizes healthy eating, regular physical activity, weight management when needed, and gradual behavior changes that can be maintained over time.

For people with diabetes, physical activity can help manage weight and diabetes. Being active makes the body more sensitive to insulin, the hormone that helps cells use blood sugar for energy. CDC also recommends choosing carbohydrates that are higher in fiber and lower in added sugar, such as beans and sweet potatoes, and drinking more water with fewer sweetened beverages to support blood sugar and weight goals. Diabetes prevention guidance emphasizes healthy eating, regular physical activity, weight management when needed, and gradual behavior changes that can be maintained over time.

Prediabetes means blood sugar levels are higher than normal but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes. Prediabetes increases risk for type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and stroke. CDC states that people with prediabetes can lower the risk of developing type 2 diabetes by eating healthy, being more active, and losing weight. CDC-recognized diabetes prevention programs can provide additional support. Diabetes prevention guidance emphasizes healthy eating, regular physical activity, weight management when needed, and gradual behavior changes that can be maintained over time.

Physical activity can help people with arthritis reduce joint pain and improve function and mood. Adults, including those with arthritis, need a mix of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activity. Physical activity can be broken into short sessions, such as 5 or 10 minutes at a time. Joint-friendly activities are enjoyable, easy to access, cause no or little pain, and can be continued over time. Activity should match ability and comfort, avoid worsening pain, and can be adapted with help from a health care professional or physical activity specialist when needed.

source_title: Physical Activity for People with Disability
text: People with disabilities and chronic health conditions can benefit from regular physical activity. Physical activity can support daily living activities and independence and can lower the risk of early death, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers. Adults with disabilities or chronic health conditions can participate in physical activity, but CDC advises consulting a health care professional or physical activity specialist to understand how a condition affects safe participation. Activity should match ability and comfort, avoid worsening pain, and can be adapted with help from a health care professional or physical activity specialist when needed.

Adults with chronic health conditions or disabilities can be physically active, and regular physical activity provides many health benefits. Conditions specifically listed by CDC include hypertension and stroke, arthritis, Parkinson's disease, spinal cord injury, and type 2 diabetes. Physical activity can support daily living activities and independence, improve sleep quality, help control weight, improve mental health, and lower risk for early death, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers. Activity should match ability and comfort, avoid worsening pain, and can be adapted with help from a health care professional or physical activity specialist when needed.

Joint-friendly physical activities are activities that put no or low stress on the joints. CDC lists brisk walking, cycling, light gardening, dancing, tai chi, swimming, and water exercises as examples. For strength training, weights or resistance bands should not cause joint pain. As the body gets used to an activity, difficulty can be increased in small amounts over time. Low-impact choices can help people stay active while reducing stress on painful joints, and activity can be increased slowly as tolerance improves.

source_title: How to Measure Physical Activity Intensity
text: Moderate-intensity activities can include brisk walking, recreational swimming, bicycling slower than 10 miles per hour on level terrain, doubles tennis, active forms of yoga, ballroom or line dancing, general yard work, and water aerobics. Moderate-intensity activity raises breathing and heart rate, but a person can still talk during the activity. Activity choices can be matched to ability, comfort, and health condition. Low-impact choices can help people stay active while reducing stress on painful joints, and activity can be increased slowly as tolerance improves.

For healthy pregnant and postpartum women, moderate-intensity physical activity is safe and has health benefits during pregnancy and after birth. CDC recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week during pregnancy and the postpartum period, such as 30 minutes on 5 days. Physical activity during pregnancy can reduce risk of excessive weight gain and gestational diabetes and can help keep the heart and lungs healthy. Pregnant and postpartum people should adjust activity based on health status and pregnancy progress and discuss activity changes with a health care professional.

During the postpartum period, the first year after delivery, physical activity can decrease symptoms of postpartum depression. When combined with healthy eating, activity can also help with weight loss after delivery. Examples of physical activity during and after pregnancy include brisk walking, some forms of yoga, water aerobics, and bike riding. After the first trimester, CDC advises avoiding activities that require lying flat on the back. Pregnant and postpartum people should adjust activity based on health status and pregnancy progress and discuss activity changes with a health care professional.

WHO recommends that pregnant and postpartum women without contraindication undertake regular physical activity throughout pregnancy and postpartum. They should do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity throughout the week for substantial health benefits. WHO also recommends incorporating a variety of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities, and adding gentle stretching may also be beneficial. Women who were physically active before pregnancy can continue activity during pregnancy and postpartum when appropriate. Pregnant and postpartum people should adjust activity based on health status and pregnancy progress and discuss activity changes with a health care professional.

Sugary drinks are a leading source of added sugars in the American diet. They include regular soda, fruit drinks, sports drinks, energy drinks, sweetened waters, flavored coffees, and sweet drinks ordered when eating out. Adults who often drink sugary drinks are more likely to experience weight gain, obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, cavities, and gout. Reading nutrition labels can help identify drinks with high added sugar. Limiting sugary drinks can reduce added sugar intake and support healthier dietary patterns, weight management, and lower risk of diet-related health problems.

source_title: Get the Facts: Sugar-Sweetened Beverages and Consumption
text: Sugar-sweetened beverages are liquids sweetened with added sugars such as corn syrup, dextrose, fructose, glucose, honey, maltose, molasses, raw sugar, or sucrose. Examples include regular soda, fruit drinks, sports drinks, energy drinks, sweetened waters, and coffee or tea beverages with added sugars. Frequently drinking sugar-sweetened beverages is associated with weight gain, obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, tooth decay, and cavities. Limiting sugary drinks can support healthy weight and healthy eating patterns. Limiting sugary drinks can reduce added sugar intake and support healthier dietary patterns, weight management, and lower risk of diet-related health problems.

Drinking excessively increases the risk of getting sick, injured, or dying sooner. People can choose not to drink, drink less, or drink in moderation to lower these risks compared with drinking excessively. CDC defines moderate drinking as two drinks or fewer in a day for men and one drink or fewer in a day for women. Even moderate drinking may increase risk of death and other alcohol-related harms compared with not drinking. People can choose not to drink, drink less, or stay within moderation limits to reduce alcohol-related risks compared with excessive drinking.

source_title: Alcohol Use Effects on Men’s and Women’s Health
text: Alcohol can affect any part of the body, and excessive alcohol use increases the risk of disease, injury, and earlier death. The body’s ability to process alcohol depends on factors such as amount consumed, time between drinks, alcohol tolerance, whether a person has eaten, medicines or other drugs, body size and weight, and body composition. These factors can differ by sex and can lead to differences in alcohol processing and health effects. People can choose not to drink, drink less, or stay within moderation limits to reduce alcohol-related risks compared with excessive drinking.

Quitting smoking has health benefits at any age, no matter how long or how much a person has smoked. Quitting improves health and quality of life, reduces risk of premature death, and reduces risk for cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cancer, and poor reproductive health outcomes. Quitting smoking is one of the most important actions people can take to improve health. Quitting support can include counseling and proven treatments, and quitting benefits health even for people who have smoked for many years.

Quitting smoking is one of the most important steps a person can take to improve health, regardless of age or how long they have smoked. Nicotine addiction can make quitting difficult, but CDC states that proven treatments can help. Counseling can help people make a quit plan, and using counseling with medication gives people who smoke the best chance of quitting for good. Quitting support can include counseling and proven treatments, and quitting benefits health even for people who have smoked for many years.

Good sleep is essential for health and emotional well-being. CDC lists recommended daily sleep by age group; adults ages 18 to 60 need 7 or more hours, adults 61 to 64 need 7 to 9 hours, and adults 65 and older need 7 to 8 hours. Getting enough sleep can help people stay at a healthy weight, reduce stress, improve mood, improve heart health and metabolism, and lower risk of chronic conditions. Consistent sleep schedules, a quiet and relaxing bedroom, less screen exposure before bed, and avoiding late caffeine or alcohol can support better sleep quality.

Better sleep habits can help people get a good night’s sleep. CDC recommends going to bed and getting up at the same time every day, keeping the bedroom quiet, relaxing, and cool, turning off electronic devices at least 30 minutes before bedtime, avoiding large meals and alcohol before bedtime, avoiding caffeine in the afternoon or evening, exercising regularly, and maintaining a healthy diet. Consistent sleep schedules, a quiet and relaxing bedroom, less screen exposure before bed, and avoiding late caffeine or alcohol can support better sleep quality.

Adults should move more and sit less. CDC states that some physical activity is better than none, and adults who sit less and do any amount of moderate- or vigorous-intensity physical activity gain some health benefits. Physical activity can be spread across the week and broken into shorter amounts of time, which can help people who sit for long periods add movement into daily life. Replacing long sitting periods with brief movement breaks can help adults add activity without needing to complete all exercise at once.

Adults need muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days each week, in addition to aerobic activity. Muscle-strengthening activities should work the major muscle groups, including legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders, and arms. Examples can include lifting weights, using resistance bands, or other activities that make muscles work harder than usual. Strength activities can be adapted to ability and combined with weekly aerobic activity. Strengthening activities should work all major muscle groups and can be adapted with weights, resistance bands, or body-weight movements.

source_title: How to Measure Physical Activity Intensity
text: Physical activity intensity describes how hard a person works during activity and affects heart rate and breathing. CDC describes moderate-intensity activities as those that make breathing and heart rate noticeably faster while still allowing a person to talk but not sing. Examples include brisk walking, recreational swimming, bicycling on level terrain at a slower pace, doubles tennis, active yoga, dancing, yard work, and water aerobics. Moderate intensity can be judged with the talk test and includes activities that raise breathing and heart rate while still allowing conversation.

WHO describes health benefits from diets high in whole grains, vegetables, fruit, legumes, and nuts. A healthy diet protects against malnutrition and diet-related noncommunicable diseases such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and cancer. Fruit and vegetables are part of a broader healthy dietary pattern that is also low in salt, free sugars, saturated fat, and trans fat. Healthy diets support health, well-being, and development across the life course. Fruit and vegetables are part of a broader diet pattern that also includes whole grains, legumes, nuts, and lower intake of salt, sugars, and unhealthy fats.

WHO states that a healthy diet is low in fats, particularly saturated and trans fats. Diets high in whole grains, vegetables, fruit, legumes, and nuts and low in salt, free sugars, and unhealthy fats are associated with health benefits. Reducing saturated and industrially produced trans fats is one part of an overall healthy dietary pattern intended to reduce the risk of diet-related noncommunicable diseases. Reducing saturated and trans fats should occur within a balanced diet that also emphasizes whole grains, vegetables, fruit, legumes, and nuts.

WHO identifies low intake of free sugars as part of a healthy diet. A healthy dietary pattern emphasizes whole grains, vegetables, fruit, legumes, and nuts and limits salt, free sugars, saturated fats, and trans fats. Reducing free sugars should be considered together with other diet improvements rather than as an isolated rule. Diets high in healthier foods and low in sugars and unhealthy fats help protect against diet-related noncommunicable diseases. Lower free sugar intake should be combined with healthier food choices and reduced intake of other diet risk factors such as excess salt and unhealthy fats.
